findings.issue_text: [BUG] The diff adds `var ErrDeviceLimitReached = fmt.Errorf("device limit reached")` but shows no addition of "fmt" to the import block (the import hunk only closes it), so the file does not compile. Build of pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore fails with 'undefined: fmt' unless fmt was already imported (no evidence it was), breaking CI and all downstream packages.

[BUG] ProvideAnonDBStore's signature gains a new `deviceLimit int64` parameter, but every other registration/call site of this provider outside this diff (fx/wire registration of the anon store) is not updated, leaving a DI graph that can no longer supply the new int64 argument. Grafana constructs providers via fx; a ProvideAnonDBStore registered through fx.Provide now requires an int64 that the container does not provide (the value lives inside *setting.Cfg, not as a standalone int64), so the server fails at startup with a dependency-injection error even though impl.go builds its own instance manually.

[BUG] updateDevice passes the SQL query string as args[0] to dbSession.Exec, i.e. `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)` then `dbSession.Exec(args...)`, relying on sqlx-style Exec(sqlOrArgs...) accepting the query as the first variadic element; with the sqlstore DBSession wrapper this dispatches the query as a bound parameter rather than a statement. If DBSession.Exec does not treat the first variadic element as the query, every device-limit-exceeded update fails with a SQL syntax/bind error, and CreateOrUpdateDevice returns a raw SQL error instead of ErrDeviceLimitReached, so anonymous authentication breaks whenever the configured limit is hit.

[BUG] Removing the background goroutine makes TagDevice run synchronously on the anonymous authentication hot path, and the deleted recover() means a panic in TagDevice now propagates into the request handler instead of being logged. Every anonymous request pays the CountDevices SQL query plus UPDATE latency before authenticating (the old code deliberately made this fire-and-forget with a 2-minute timeout and panic guard); a panic in device tagging now crashes the request goroutine and returns a 500 to anonymous users who previously succeeded.

[BUG] The diff adds no verification of what HTTP response an anonymous user receives when Authenticate returns ErrDeviceLimitReached — no test covers the client.Authenticate error path, and no mapping of the error to a status code or message exists anywhere in the diff. Once the device limit is reached, new anonymous devices get whatever the generic authn error handler produces (likely 500-style internal error rather than an explanatory 4xx), and a regression here is invisible because the only new test (TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit) stops at the store layer; database_test.go and impl_test.go in this diff contain no assertion on the Authenticate/TagDevice rejection behavior.

[BUG] The count-then-insert limit check is not atomic: two concurrent CreateOrUpdateDevice calls for new devices can both read count < deviceLimit and both insert, exceeding the configured limit. Operators setting device_limit=N can end up with materially more than N devices under burst load, silently violating the limit the feature promises; no test in database_test.go covers concurrent inserts.

[ADVISORY] TagDevice's error-handling contract changed from log-only to error-returning, but other callers of TagDevice besides the Anonymous client (e.g., the post-login untagDevice hook path and any API/render tagging) are not updated or tested for the new error propagation. Callers that previously tolerated tag failures (the local-cache-miss path in tagDeviceUI, the untag hook) now surface errors up paths whose handlers were never written to expect them; the diff's impl_test.go tests only exercise the no-error happy path.

[ADVISORY] anonymousDeviceLimit is plumbed through the frontend config type, GrafanaBootConfig default, and FrontendSettingsDTO, but no frontend code in this diff reads it — a ships-inert public surface field. Three files carry a serialized setting no consumer uses; the bytes cross the frontend-settings payload every request and any future shape change (e.g., string vs number) has no consumer to catch drift.

[ADVISORY] The new device_limit ini key is read but no default is documented in conf/defaults.ini and no example/comment is added anywhere, and no test verifies the ini parsing of device_limit (including negative or zero values). Operators cannot discover the setting exists (defaults.ini is Grafana's documented config surface), and a negative value silently disables the limit (deviceLimit > 0 check) with no validation or warning.

[ADVISORY] updateDevice's SQL is built by prepending the query string into the args slice and passing it to Exec instead of using the query/args parameters directly, and the query matches rows by device_id AND an updated_at window that overlaps the count window but uses a hard-coded 1-minute future slack. The next maintainer editing this function must understand the unusual query-in-args convention (drift-prone), and the hard-coded time.Minute slack combined with per-request time.Now() calls means a device whose updated_at is more than 1 minute in the future (clock skew) is spuriously rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached even though it exists.

[ADVISORY] TagDevice was moved from a fire-and-forget background goroutine (with its own detached 2-minute timeout) to a synchronous call on the anonymous authentication path. Every anonymous page load now blocks on a DB count query (when deviceLimit > 0) plus a DB write before authentication completes; operators enabling the limit add per-request DB latency to all anonymous traffic, and request-context cancellation now silently drops device tags that previously survived via context.Background(), undercounting active devices.

[ADVISORY] The device-limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert: CountDevices and the subsequent upsert run in separate sessions with no transaction, unique constraint, or lock. Two concurrent anonymous requests (or two Grafana instances behind a load balancer, since the count is per-DB but not serialized) both observe count < deviceLimit and both insert, so the configured limit is exceeded whenever traffic bursts; operators relying on device_limit as a hard cap get no enforcement.

[ADVISORY] AnonymousDeviceLimit is plumbed all the way to the frontend settings DTO and the TS GrafanaConfig type, but nothing in this diff reads it client-side. The config key ships as an inert field on every frontend boot payload; the next maintainer cannot tell whether any UI behavior depends on it, and if the intended UX is to warn blocked anonymous users, that requirement has no implementation traceable to this diff.

[ADVISORY] Authenticate returns the raw anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached to the authn layer with no mapping to an HTTP status or user-facing message. Anonymous users who exceed the device limit get whatever generic error authn produces for a client error (typically a 500-style internal error) instead of a deliberate 403/429 with an explanation, and API consumers cannot distinguish 'limit reached' from a server fault; the diff adds the failure path but no requirement defining the response contract.

[BUG] The device limit is enforced with a check-then-act pattern: a SELECT COUNT followed by a separate insert/update, with no unique constraint or transactional guard, so the limit is racy. N concurrent anonymous authentication requests all read count < deviceLimit and all insert, overshooting the configured limit by up to N-1 devices per race window; the limit is a soft suggestion, not an invariant.

[ADVISORY] updateDevice overloads ErrDeviceLimitReached to mean 'row not found or updated_at outside the window', conflating three distinct outcomes under one sentinel. A device that exists but whose updated_at is stale (e.g. clock skew past the +1min upper bound, or a device inactive >30 days that DeleteDevicesOlderThan hasn't reaped yet) gets ErrDeviceLimitReached instead of being treated as a new device, so that browser is permanently locked out of anonymous access until the cleanup job runs; the API layer also returns this error verbatim to an unauthenticated end user.

[ADVISORY] TagDevice was moved from a background goroutine with a 2-minute timeout to a synchronous, un-timeouted call on the anonymous authentication hot path. Every anonymous request that misses the 29-minute local cache now performs a COUNT query plus insert/update inline in Authenticate with no timeout; a slow or saturated database adds that latency directly to anonymous page loads and, because Authenticate now returns the error, a DB hiccup during the count returns an auth failure rather than logging and proceeding as before.

[ADVISORY] The 30-day expiration constant is now defined twice in sibling packages (anonstore.anonymousDeviceExpiration and anonimpl.anonymousDeviceExpiration) with no single source of truth. The next editor tuning the retention window updates one copy (e.g. the delete job's) but not the store's limit-window copy, and the count used for limit enforcement silently disagrees with the deletion window, admitting or rejecting devices on a stale horizon.

[ADVISORY] AnonymousDeviceLimit is serialized unconditionally with no omitempty, exposing the raw server-side limit (including the 0-means-unlimited encoding) to every anonymous, unauthenticated client via /api/frontend-settings, while the frontend type declares it number | undefined. Unauthenticated users can read the operator's configured device limit (an operational-detail leak), and the frontend's `undefined` branch is dead code since the backend always sends a number — the undefined case can never represent 'not yet loaded', which is exactly the sentinel confusion the type invites.

[BUG] The PR's stated intent is 'add configurable device limit', but the implementation converts a device-tracking limit into an authentication denial: when ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned, Authenticate returns the error and the anonymous user is refused access entirely, instead of proceeding with an untracked session as the previous design (fire-and-forget goroutine, errors only logged) guaranteed. An operator setting device_limit to N causes anonymous visitor N+1 onward to get an auth failure/HTTP error on Grafana instead of anonymous access — the limit silently became a deny-list for anonymous users, an objective change far beyond 'limit stored devices'.

[BUG] updateDevice's WHERE clause requires updated_at within the last 30 days (device.UpdatedAt - anonymousDeviceExpiration to +1min), so a returning anonymous user whose device cookie was last seen more than 30 days ago gets 0 rows affected and ErrDeviceLimitReached, which client.go now propagates as a hard authentication failure. A legitimate returning anonymous user (inactive >30 days) is locked out of Grafana whenever the device limit is reached and their stale row still exists but falls outside the update window — the 'only update existing devices' fallback fails exactly for the devices it is meant to keep.

[ADVISORY] The diff removes the async goroutine, its 2-minute context.WithTimeout, and the recover() panic guard that were explicit accepted constraints of the original tagging design, making TagDevice synchronous on the anonymous auth hot path with no timeout and no panic isolation. Every anonymous request now blocks on a DB read (CountDevices) plus write (insert/update) before responding — a DB slowdown directly degrades all anonymous page loads, and a panic inside TagDevice now takes down the auth request handler instead of being logged and swallowed as the original code deliberately did.

[BUG] TagDevice now returns errors from tagDeviceUI (previously only logged at Debug and returned nil), which combined with client.go's propagation turns any transient DB error during device tagging into a failed anonymous authentication. A transient database error on the anon_device table (previously tolerated by design — logged, auth proceeded) now returns 500s to every anonymous user, changing the accepted failure contract of anonymous auth.

[ADVISORY] anonymousDeviceLimit is plumbed all the way through GrafanaBootConfig and the FrontendSettingsDTO, but no code in this diff consumes it on the frontend, making the frontend exposure a ships-inert surface. Frontend developers/bundlers carry a dead config field; if the intent was to show a device-limit notice in the UI, that behavior is absent and the field is payload with no reader.

[ADVISORY] Returning ErrDeviceLimitReached from Authenticate turns the anonymous device limit into a global denial-of-service vector against anonymous access. An attacker sends requests with varied IPs/user-agents (each producing a distinct device_id via TagDevice) until the 30-day device count reaches AnonymousDeviceLimit; from then on every new anonymous user's Authenticate call fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached, locking out all legitimate anonymous viewers for up to 30 days with no automatic recovery short of DB cleanup or config change.

[ADVISORY] The device-limit check is a check-then-act race: CountDevices and the subsequent insert run in separate sessions with no locking, unique constraint on the counted window, or transaction, so concurrent requests exceed the configured limit. Operators who set device_limit as a resource/cost control see it silently violated under concurrent load (N concurrent anonymous requests all read count below the limit and all insert), and since the limit now also gates authentication, the same race makes the enforcement guarantee unenforceable as a security boundary.

[ADVISORY] updateDevice lets an unauthenticated caller overwrite the client_ip and user_agent of any existing device row within the expiry window, keyed solely on the client-supplied device_id with no ownership or verification check. Once the limit is reached, any anonymous request whose derived device_id collides with an existing active device rewrites that device's recorded IP/UA, so an attacker can poison the audit/telemetry records of other anonymous users; combined with the count race above, the update path also becomes the only write path, making the poisoning reliable.

[ADVISORY] Publishing AnonymousDeviceLimit in the public frontend settings DTO discloses an internal capacity-control value to every unauthenticated visitor. An anonymous attacker learns the exact device_limit, letting them compute precisely how many distinct device_ids to generate to saturate the limit and trigger the global anonymous-auth denial described in the client.go finding.

[ADVISORY] The only new test for the device-limit path never exercises the updateDevice success branch, only its failure branch via a nonexistent device. TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit passes device_id "keep" that was never inserted, so updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached because rowsAffected==0 for a missing row — the same error would fire if the UPDATE's WHERE clause were subtly wrong (e.g. the BETWEEN window or column mismatch). The intended new behavior — that an existing device within the 30-day window IS updated when the limit is reached — is never asserted, so a regression that makes limit-reached updates always fail (locking all anonymous users out, not just new ones) ships green. A second assertion creating device "keep" first and requiring NoError would cover it.

[ADVISORY] The new errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached) branch in Authenticate, which turns a device-limit condition into a hard authentication failure, has no test in the diff. Checked the diff's test files (database_test.go, impl_test.go): neither constructs an Anonymous client nor calls Authenticate, and impl_test.go's TagDevice tests all require.NoError — none drives ErrDeviceLimitReached through the service. The new deny-path (anonymous request rejected with an error instead of logging a warning) is unverified; a regression here (e.g. the errors.Is check matching nothing and falling through to log.Warn, silently admitting users past the configured limit) passes the existing suite.

[ADVISORY] The newly added `return err` in TagDevice after tagDeviceUI failure — a behavior change that surfaces UI-tag errors to callers (previously swallowed and only logged) — is not exercised by any test, since every TagDevice call in impl_test.go's testCases succeeds. impl_test.go's testCases table only contains requests that tag successfully and require.NoError on each call; no case injects a store failure to trigger the new return. A regression that returns errors for previously-tolerated conditions (e.g. a wrapped error that no longer matches errors.Is(ErrDeviceLimitReached) in client.go, breaking the intended distinction between limit-reached and transient failures) is invisible to the suite. The test table mirrors the code's happy path rather than the spec's error semantics.

[BUG] updateDevice conflates 'no eligible row updated' with ErrDeviceLimitReached, so a known device whose updated_at is older than 30 days (expired from the window but not yet deleted by the cleanup job) fails authentication with a device-limit error. A returning anonymous user whose device row exists but has updated_at outside [UpdatedAt-30d, UpdatedAt+1min] gets rowsAffected==0, and CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached; client.go then rejects the authentication even though the device limit was never the trigger — returning visitors are randomly locked out depending on cleanup-job timing.

[BUG] ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned raw from the authn client's Authenticate, surfacing an internal store error as an undefined auth failure (authn's generic error handling, i.e. a 500/internal error) instead of any defined 4xx response for an over-limit anonymous device. An anonymous visitor hitting the device limit gets an unauthenticated internal-error-shaped response rather than a defined limit-exceeded response; the error path is also the first time this error type crosses the authn boundary with no mapping registered for it.

[BUG] TagDevice was moved from a fire-and-forget goroutine with a 2-minute timeout onto the synchronous critical path of every anonymous authentication, adding two DB round trips (CountDevices + insert/update) to each anonymous request with no timeout of its own. Every anonymous page view now blocks on the anon_device count query plus a write before the identity is returned; a slow or degraded database directly increases latency for all anonymous traffic that previously authenticated without waiting, and the 2-minute timeout that bounded the old async tag is gone entirely.

[BUG] TagDevice now returns the tagDeviceUI error instead of only logging it, so any DB failure in the UI-tagging path propagates out of TagDevice on the synchronous request path. Combined with the now-synchronous call in client.go, a transient anon_device DB error (previously a debug log plus successful auth) now surfaces as a logged warning per request but, for any future caller that checks the error, turns a degraded-tagging condition into an auth-path error; the behavior change from debug-log to returned error is unhandled by the only caller's non-limit branch.

[ADVISORY] The device-limit check is a check-then-act race: CountDevices is read outside any transaction with the subsequent insert, so concurrent anonymous requests can all observe count < deviceLimit and insert, exceeding the configured limit. Operators setting device_limit get a soft limit that overshoots under bursty anonymous traffic; there is no unique constraint or atomic guard enforcing the cap, and the overshoot is silent (no log when it happens).

[ADVISORY] CountDevices is executed on every CreateOrUpdateDevice call whenever deviceLimit > 0, adding an unconditional count query (a full scan over the 30-day window rows on large deployments) to the per-request path. Deployments with millions of anon_device rows pay a counted range scan per anonymous request before any cache/local-cache check short-circuits the write; the count is not cached or rate-limited, so the limit feature converts anonymous auth into count-query amplification proportional to traffic.

[ADVISORY] anonymousDeviceLimit is serialized into frontend settings but nothing in this diff consumes it client-side, so the setting ships inert on the frontend. The value is broadcast to every browser session with no reader; if a UI limit indicator was intended, it is absent, and the field will either rot or require a follow-up to become usable — meanwhile the setting is already fully server-enforced.

goldens.comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `updateDevice` prepending the SQL string into a `[]interface{}` and calling `dbSession.Exec(args...)`. This strongly implies `DBSession.Exec` is a variadic-only API (xorm-style `Exec(sqlOrArgs ...interface{})`) that expects the query as the first variadic element; otherwise this code would not even compile if `Exec` had the common `Exec(query string, args ...any)` signature. Additionally, the new integration test `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` exercises the device-limit path (which calls `updateDevice`) and asserts `ErrDeviceLimitReached`; if `Exec` treated the first element as a bound parameter and caused a SQL/bind error, this test would fail. The finding’s claim about how `DBSession.Exec` dispatches parameters is not verifiable from the diff and is contradicted by the presence of a test covering this path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does remove the fire-and-forget goroutine in `Anonymous.Authenticate` and the associated `recover()`/2-minute timeout (`pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go`), replacing it with a synchronous `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...)` call. These are concrete perf/robustness concerns on the auth hot path. However, parts of the finding overstate what’s provable from the diff (e.g., it’s not necessarily “every anonymous request” due to local caching, and whether a panic would yield a 500 depends on higher-level recovery not shown), so it’s better classified as a non-bug but important review issue rather than a definite defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new device_limit ini key is read but no default is documented in conf/defaults.ini and no example/comment is added anywhere, and no test verifies the ini parsing of device_limit (including negative or zero values). Operators cannot discover the setting exists (defaults.ini is Grafana's documented config surface), and a negative value silently disables the limit (deviceLimit > 0 check) with no validation or warning.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add parsing for `auth.anonymous.device_limit` (`cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)`), but there’s no accompanying validation or warning for negative values and the limit logic only triggers on `s.deviceLimit > 0` (in `CreateOrUpdateDevice`), so negative values silently disable enforcement. Also, the new/changed tests exercise the DB store limit behavior, but none verify INI parsing behavior for `device_limit` (e.g., default/zero/negative cases). The claim about missing documentation in `conf/defaults.ini` is not verifiable from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] updateDevice's SQL is built by prepending the query string into the args slice and passing it to Exec instead of using the query/args parameters directly, and the query matches rows by device_id AND an updated_at window that overlaps the count window but uses a hard-coded 1-minute future slack. The next maintainer editing this function must understand the unusual query-in-args convention (drift-prone), and the hard-coded time.Minute slack combined with per-request time.Now() calls means a device whose updated_at is more than 1 minute in the future (clock skew) is spuriously rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached even though it exists.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `updateDevice` building `args` by prepending the SQL string and then calling `dbSession.Exec(args...)` (instead of `Exec(query, args...)`), which is an unusual/opaque convention and could be drift-prone for maintainers. The diff also hard-codes a `time.Minute` upper-bound slack in the `updated_at BETWEEN ... AND ...` predicate and uses different time anchors (`device.UpdatedAt` in `updateDevice` vs `time.Now()` in `CountDevices`), which is a concrete, diff-grounded maintainability/edge-case concern. However, the specific claim that a device with `updated_at` > 1 minute in the future is spuriously rejected is not directly verified from the shown logic (the BETWEEN window is based on `device.UpdatedAt`, not `time.Now()`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] TagDevice was moved from a fire-and-forget background goroutine (with its own detached 2-minute timeout) to a synchronous call on the anonymous authentication path. Every anonymous page load now blocks on a DB count query (when deviceLimit > 0) plus a DB write before authentication completes; operators enabling the limit add per-request DB latency to all anonymous traffic, and request-context cancellation now silently drops device tags that previously survived via context.Background(), undercounting active devices.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows Anonymous.Authenticate removed the fire-and-forget goroutine and detached context timeout (previously `go ... context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), ...)`) and now calls `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...)` synchronously on the auth path (pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go). With `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit > 0`, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` performs a `CountDevices(...)` query and then a DB update/insert (pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go), so anonymous requests can now block on DB I/O. Also, because the call now uses the request context, cancellations/timeouts can prevent tagging in cases where it previously would proceed under `context.Background()`. This is a real, diff-grounded behavioral/performance concern, but not a clearly verifiable correctness defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The device-limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert: CountDevices and the subsequent upsert run in separate sessions with no transaction, unique constraint, or lock. Two concurrent anonymous requests (or two Grafana instances behind a load balancer, since the count is per-DB but not serialized) both observe count < deviceLimit and both insert, so the configured limit is exceeded whenever traffic bursts; operators relying on device_limit as a hard cap get no enforcement.
matched_golden_ids: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate describes the same race condition: a non-atomic count-then-insert/upsert without transaction/locking allows concurrent requests to bypass the device limit and create more devices than allowed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] AnonymousDeviceLimit is plumbed all the way to the frontend settings DTO and the TS GrafanaConfig type, but nothing in this diff reads it client-side. The config key ships as an inert field on every frontend boot payload; the next maintainer cannot tell whether any UI behavior depends on it, and if the intended UX is to warn blocked anonymous users, that requirement has no implementation traceable to this diff.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly adds `AnonymousDeviceLimit`/`anonymousDeviceLimit` to the backend `FrontendSettingsDTO` (`pkg/api/dtos/frontend_settings.go`) and TS `GrafanaConfig`/`GrafanaBootConfig` (`packages/grafana-data/...` and `packages/grafana-runtime/...`), meaning it will be included in the frontend boot payload. Within this diff, the value is only *produced* (read from `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` and sent to the DTO) and not *consumed* by any frontend/client-side logic shown here, so it is plausibly an inert field that could confuse maintainers about intended UX/behavior. This is not a correctness defect (server-side limit is enforced in `CreateOrUpdateDevice`), but it is a diff-grounded scope/clarity concern about exposing an apparently-unused setting to the client.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Authenticate returns the raw anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached to the authn layer with no mapping to an HTTP status or user-facing message. Anonymous users who exceed the device limit get whatever generic error authn produces for a client error (typically a 500-style internal error) instead of a deliberate 403/429 with an explanation, and API consumers cannot distinguish 'limit reached' from a server fault; the diff adds the failure path but no requirement defining the response contract.

[BUG] The device limit is enforced with a check-then-act pattern: a SELECT COUNT followed by a separate insert/update, with no unique constraint or transactional guard, so the limit is racy. N concurrent anonymous authentication requests all read count < deviceLimit and all insert, overshooting the configured limit by up to N-1 devices per race window; the limit is a soft suggestion, not an invariant.

adjudication.rationale: In `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, the limit check is implemented as `CountDevices(...)` followed by a separate insert/upsert path when `count < s.deviceLimit` (pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go). There is no transaction or locking shown that ties the count to the subsequent write, so concurrent requests can all observe `count < limit` and each insert a new device, overshooting the intended limit. The diff also doesn’t show any DB-level constraint that would prevent this (the limit is not enforceable via a unique key), so the finding about a racy check-then-act limit is verifiable from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] updateDevice overloads ErrDeviceLimitReached to mean 'row not found or updated_at outside the window', conflating three distinct outcomes under one sentinel. A device that exists but whose updated_at is stale (e.g. clock skew past the +1min upper bound, or a device inactive >30 days that DeleteDevicesOlderThan hasn't reaped yet) gets ErrDeviceLimitReached instead of being treated as a new device, so that browser is permanently locked out of anonymous access until the cleanup job runs; the API layer also returns this error verbatim to an unauthenticated end user.

[ADVISORY] TagDevice was moved from a background goroutine with a 2-minute timeout to a synchronous, un-timeouted call on the anonymous authentication hot path. Every anonymous request that misses the 29-minute local cache now performs a COUNT query plus insert/update inline in Authenticate with no timeout; a slow or saturated database adds that latency directly to anonymous page loads and, because Authenticate now returns the error, a DB hiccup during the count returns an auth failure rather than logging and proceeding as before.

[ADVISORY] The 30-day expiration constant is now defined twice in sibling packages (anonstore.anonymousDeviceExpiration and anonimpl.anonymousDeviceExpiration) with no single source of truth. The next editor tuning the retention window updates one copy (e.g. the delete job's) but not the store's limit-window copy, and the count used for limit enforcement silently disagrees with the deletion window, admitting or rejecting devices on a stale horizon.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce two separate 30-day constants: `const anonymousDeviceExpiration = 30 * 24 * time.Hour` in `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go` (used for limit-window counting and update-window) and another `const anonymousDeviceExpiration = 30 * 24 * time.Hour` in `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/api/api.go` (used for `ListDevices` time range). This duplication is real and could cause future inconsistency if one is changed without the other, but as shown they currently match and there’s no verifiable incorrect behavior in this diff right now.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] AnonymousDeviceLimit is serialized unconditionally with no omitempty, exposing the raw server-side limit (including the 0-means-unlimited encoding) to every anonymous, unauthenticated client via /api/frontend-settings, while the frontend type declares it number | undefined. Unauthenticated users can read the operator's configured device limit (an operational-detail leak), and the frontend's `undefined` branch is dead code since the backend always sends a number — the undefined case can never represent 'not yet loaded', which is exactly the sentinel confusion the type invites.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the backend always includes `AnonymousDeviceLimit` in `FrontendSettingsDTO` as a plain `int64` with `json:"anonymousDeviceLimit"` (no `omitempty`) and always sets it in `getFrontendSettings` (`AnonymousDeviceLimit: hs.Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit`). That means `/api/frontend-settings` will always serialize a number (including `0`), while the TS config type was added as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined` and the boot config default is `undefined`, creating a mismatch/inconsistent sentinel semantics. However, whether exposing this limit to unauthenticated clients is an actual security defect isn’t provable from the diff alone (the endpoint is intended for frontend bootstrapping and already exposes other settings), so it’s better classified as an API/design concern rather than a definite bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The PR's stated intent is 'add configurable device limit', but the implementation converts a device-tracking limit into an authentication denial: when ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned, Authenticate returns the error and the anonymous user is refused access entirely, instead of proceeding with an untracked session as the previous design (fire-and-forget goroutine, errors only logged) guaranteed. An operator setting device_limit to N causes anonymous visitor N+1 onward to get an auth failure/HTTP error on Grafana instead of anonymous access — the limit silently became a deny-list for anonymous users, an objective change far beyond 'limit stored devices'.
matched_golden_ids: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags that ErrDeviceLimitReached from TagDevice now causes Authenticate to return an error, denying anonymous access, whereas previously device tagging was fire-and-forget and non-blocking (errors only logged). This is the same regression described in the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] updateDevice's WHERE clause requires updated_at within the last 30 days (device.UpdatedAt - anonymousDeviceExpiration to +1min), so a returning anonymous user whose device cookie was last seen more than 30 days ago gets 0 rows affected and ErrDeviceLimitReached, which client.go now propagates as a hard authentication failure. A legitimate returning anonymous user (inactive >30 days) is locked out of Grafana whenever the device limit is reached and their stale row still exists but falls outside the update window — the 'only update existing devices' fallback fails exactly for the devices it is meant to keep.
matched_golden_ids: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Yes. The candidate explains that updateDevice’s WHERE clause can yield 0 rows affected (e.g., device outside the 30-day updated_at window / effectively not matching), yet the code maps that to ErrDeviceLimitReached. This is the same core bug as the golden comment: 0 affected rows means “no matching device/update window miss,” not “device limit reached.”

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The diff removes the async goroutine, its 2-minute context.WithTimeout, and the recover() panic guard that were explicit accepted constraints of the original tagging design, making TagDevice synchronous on the anonymous auth hot path with no timeout and no panic isolation. Every anonymous request now blocks on a DB read (CountDevices) plus write (insert/update) before responding — a DB slowdown directly degrades all anonymous page loads, and a panic inside TagDevice now takes down the auth request handler instead of being logged and swallowed as the original code deliberately did.

adjudication.rationale: The diff in `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go` removes the goroutine, the `context.WithTimeout(..., 2*time.Minute)` wrapper, and the `recover()` guard, and now calls `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...)` synchronously inside `Authenticate`. That makes tagging part of the auth hot path and relies on the passed `ctx` for cancellation (no explicit timeout here), and any panic inside `TagDevice` would now propagate to the caller rather than being swallowed/logged locally. Additionally, the new device-limit logic in `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go` can add a DB `CountDevices` query before write when `deviceLimit > 0`. This is a concrete performance/robustness regression risk grounded in the diff, though not a strictly provable functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] TagDevice now returns errors from tagDeviceUI (previously only logged at Debug and returned nil), which combined with client.go's propagation turns any transient DB error during device tagging into a failed anonymous authentication. A transient database error on the anon_device table (previously tolerated by design — logged, auth proceeded) now returns 500s to every anonymous user, changing the accepted failure contract of anonymous auth.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does make TagDevice return the error from tagDeviceUI (impl.go: it now `return err` after logging). However, client.go does NOT propagate “any transient DB error” to fail anonymous authentication: in Authenticate, it only returns an error when `errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached)`. All other TagDevice errors are merely logged (`a.log.Warn(...)`) and authentication proceeds. Therefore the claim that transient anon_device DB errors now cause 500s/failed anonymous auth is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] anonymousDeviceLimit is plumbed all the way through GrafanaBootConfig and the FrontendSettingsDTO, but no code in this diff consumes it on the frontend, making the frontend exposure a ships-inert surface. Frontend developers/bundlers carry a dead config field; if the intent was to show a device-limit notice in the UI, that behavior is absent and the field is payload with no reader.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly plumbs a new `anonymousDeviceLimit` value from `setting.Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` into the frontend settings payload (`FrontendSettingsDTO.AnonymousDeviceLimit` and `getFrontendSettings`), and adds corresponding TS config surface (`GrafanaConfig` / `GrafanaBootConfig`). Within this diff, there is no frontend-side consumption/behavior change tied to this new field (only backend/store logic uses the limit), so exposing it to the frontend appears potentially unnecessary/incomplete and increases the config/API surface without demonstrated use.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Returning ErrDeviceLimitReached from Authenticate turns the anonymous device limit into a global denial-of-service vector against anonymous access. An attacker sends requests with varied IPs/user-agents (each producing a distinct device_id via TagDevice) until the 30-day device count reaches AnonymousDeviceLimit; from then on every new anonymous user's Authenticate call fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached, locking out all legitimate anonymous viewers for up to 30 days with no automatic recovery short of DB cleanup or config change.

adjudication.rationale: The diff makes anonymous authentication fail when tagging the device hits the limit: `Authenticate` now calls `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...)` synchronously and explicitly returns the error when `errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached)` (pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go). The store enforces the limit by counting devices in the last 30 days and, once `count >= s.deviceLimit`, calling `updateDevice`; for a new (previously unseen) device_id this `UPDATE ... WHERE device_id = ?` affects 0 rows and returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` (pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go). This error now propagates all the way back to `Authenticate`, preventing anonymous identities from being issued for new devices after the cap is reached, effectively allowing a single party to exhaust the limit and lock out subsequent legitimate anonymous users until records expire/are cleaned/config changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The device-limit check is a check-then-act race: CountDevices and the subsequent insert run in separate sessions with no locking, unique constraint on the counted window, or transaction, so concurrent requests exceed the configured limit. Operators who set device_limit as a resource/cost control see it silently violated under concurrent load (N concurrent anonymous requests all read count below the limit and all insert), and since the limit now also gates authentication, the same race makes the enforcement guarantee unenforceable as a security boundary.

adjudication.rationale: In `AnonDBStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`, the limit enforcement does a classic check-then-act: it calls `CountDevices(...)` and, if below `s.deviceLimit`, proceeds to insert/update the device via separate DB work (the insert/upsert logic later in the method). The diff shows no transaction wrapping the count + insert, no locking, and no unique/constraint-based enforcement, so concurrent requests can all observe `count < limit` and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. Since `Anonymous.Authenticate` now returns an error on `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached`, this non-atomic enforcement can be violated/behave inconsistently under load.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] updateDevice lets an unauthenticated caller overwrite the client_ip and user_agent of any existing device row within the expiry window, keyed solely on the client-supplied device_id with no ownership or verification check. Once the limit is reached, any anonymous request whose derived device_id collides with an existing active device rewrites that device's recorded IP/UA, so an attacker can poison the audit/telemetry records of other anonymous users; combined with the count race above, the update path also becomes the only write path, making the poisoning reliable.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `updateDevice` path that runs when `deviceLimit` is reached (`CreateOrUpdateDevice` calls `s.updateDevice(ctx, device)` when `count >= s.deviceLimit`). That `UPDATE` statement overwrites `client_ip` and `user_agent` for any row matching only `device_id` (plus a time window on `updated_at`): `WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?`. There is no additional ownership/verification check in the store/API layer shown, and tagging is invoked for anonymous requests (`Anonymous.Authenticate` calls `TagDevice`). This means any anonymous request that presents a `device.DeviceID` equal to an existing active row can rewrite that row’s IP/UA, enabling poisoning of the stored telemetry/audit data once the limit forces the update-only behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Publishing AnonymousDeviceLimit in the public frontend settings DTO discloses an internal capacity-control value to every unauthenticated visitor. An anonymous attacker learns the exact device_limit, letting them compute precisely how many distinct device_ids to generate to saturate the limit and trigger the global anonymous-auth denial described in the client.go finding.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly adds `AnonymousDeviceLimit` to `FrontendSettingsDTO` (`json:"anonymousDeviceLimit"`) and populates it from `hs.Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` in `getFrontendSettings`, which is typically consumed by the unauthenticated frontend bootstrap. That does expose the configured capacity-control value to anonymous users. However, whether this is a *defect* vs an intentional UI/feature requirement isn’t provable from the diff alone (it may be needed client-side), so it’s better classified as a concrete security/architecture concern rather than a verifiable bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The only new test for the device-limit path never exercises the updateDevice success branch, only its failure branch via a nonexistent device. TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit passes device_id "keep" that was never inserted, so updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached because rowsAffected==0 for a missing row — the same error would fire if the UPDATE's WHERE clause were subtly wrong (e.g. the BETWEEN window or column mismatch). The intended new behavior — that an existing device within the 30-day window IS updated when the limit is reached — is never asserted, so a regression that makes limit-reached updates always fail (locking all anonymous users out, not just new ones) ships green. A second assertion creating device "keep" first and requiring NoError would cover it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a single new integration test, `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit`, which sets `deviceLimit` to 1, inserts one device (`DeviceID: "32mdo31deeqwes"`), then attempts a second `CreateOrUpdateDevice` after changing `DeviceID` to `"keep"` without ever inserting `"keep"` first. With the limit reached, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` calls `s.updateDevice`, whose `UPDATE ... WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?` will affect 0 rows for a missing device and returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. So the test only exercises the failure path (rowsAffected==0) and never asserts the intended success behavior (an existing device being updated when the limit is reached). This is a concrete, diff-grounded test gap rather than a proven functional defect in the implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached) branch in Authenticate, which turns a device-limit condition into a hard authentication failure, has no test in the diff. Checked the diff's test files (database_test.go, impl_test.go): neither constructs an Anonymous client nor calls Authenticate, and impl_test.go's TagDevice tests all require.NoError — none drives ErrDeviceLimitReached through the service. The new deny-path (anonymous request rejected with an error instead of logging a warning) is unverified; a regression here (e.g. the errors.Is check matching nothing and falling through to log.Warn, silently admitting users past the configured limit) passes the existing suite.

adjudication.rationale: Diff introduces new control flow in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go Authenticate: it now calls TagDevice synchronously and returns an error when errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached), turning device-limit into a hard auth failure. The added/modified tests only cover the store-level limit (TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit in database_test.go) and TagDevice happy paths in impl_test.go; none constructs an Anonymous client or calls Authenticate, and no test drives ErrDeviceLimitReached through Authenticate to verify the deny-path. This is a specific, diff-grounded missing-test gap for newly added nontrivial logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The newly added `return err` in TagDevice after tagDeviceUI failure — a behavior change that surfaces UI-tag errors to callers (previously swallowed and only logged) — is not exercised by any test, since every TagDevice call in impl_test.go's testCases succeeds. impl_test.go's testCases table only contains requests that tag successfully and require.NoError on each call; no case injects a store failure to trigger the new return. A regression that returns errors for previously-tolerated conditions (e.g. a wrapped error that no longer matches errors.Is(ErrDeviceLimitReached) in client.go, breaking the intended distinction between limit-reached and transient failures) is invisible to the suite. The test table mirrors the code's happy path rather than the spec's error semantics.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a behavior change in `AnonDeviceService.TagDevice`: after `a.tagDeviceUI(...)` fails it now `return err` (previously it only logged and then returned nil). In `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl_test.go`, the integration tests still only exercise the happy path and `require.NoError(t, err)` for every `TagDevice` call; there is no case that forces `tagDeviceUI`/store to fail to validate the new error-propagation semantics. So the finding about missing test coverage for this newly-surfaced error path is grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] updateDevice conflates 'no eligible row updated' with ErrDeviceLimitReached, so a known device whose updated_at is older than 30 days (expired from the window but not yet deleted by the cleanup job) fails authentication with a device-limit error. A returning anonymous user whose device row exists but has updated_at outside [UpdatedAt-30d, UpdatedAt+1min] gets rowsAffected==0, and CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached; client.go then rejects the authentication even though the device limit was never the trigger — returning visitors are randomly locked out depending on cleanup-job timing.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `ErrDeviceLimitReached` can only be returned from `CreateOrUpdateDevice` when the device-limit path is taken (`if s.deviceLimit > 0 { ... if count >= s.deviceLimit { return s.updateDevice(...) } }`). So the claim that “the device limit was never the trigger” is not supported by the code shown. Also, the “randomly locked out depending on cleanup-job timing” part isn’t verifiable from this diff: regardless of whether an expired row is deleted or not, once `count >= deviceLimit` the code will call `updateDevice` and reject if no eligible row matches. Whether that is intended policy (treat >30d-old devices as effectively new) cannot be concluded from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned raw from the authn client's Authenticate, surfacing an internal store error as an undefined auth failure (authn's generic error handling, i.e. a 500/internal error) instead of any defined 4xx response for an over-limit anonymous device. An anonymous visitor hitting the device limit gets an unauthenticated internal-error-shaped response rather than a defined limit-exceeded response; the error path is also the first time this error type crosses the authn boundary with no mapping registered for it.

adjudication.rationale: In `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go`, `Authenticate` now calls `TagDevice` synchronously and explicitly propagates `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` by returning `return nil, err`. `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is a store-level sentinel defined in `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go` (`fmt.Errorf("device limit reached")`) and is not wrapped/mapped to any authn-specific/typed error in this diff. While the finding’s claim about this necessarily becoming a 500/undefined HTTP response cannot be verified from the diff alone (authn error-to-HTTP mapping isn’t shown), it is verifiable that an internal storage error is crossing the authn boundary without an explicit mapping/contract.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] TagDevice was moved from a fire-and-forget goroutine with a 2-minute timeout onto the synchronous critical path of every anonymous authentication, adding two DB round trips (CountDevices + insert/update) to each anonymous request with no timeout of its own. Every anonymous page view now blocks on the anon_device count query plus a write before the identity is returned; a slow or degraded database directly increases latency for all anonymous traffic that previously authenticated without waiting, and the 2-minute timeout that bounded the old async tag is gone entirely.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a real behavioral/performance regression concern, not a clear correctness defect. In `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go`, the previous fire-and-forget goroutine with `context.WithTimeout(..., 2*time.Minute)` was removed (timeoutTag const deleted) and replaced with a synchronous `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...)` call on the authentication path. In `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go`, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` now performs an extra `CountDevices(...)` query when `deviceLimit > 0` and may then do an update/insert, meaning anonymous auth can now block on DB work with no new explicit timeout in this code. This is a diff-grounded latency/availability concern, but the diff does not prove a functional bug (authentication still returns an identity unless TagDevice errors, and lack of a timeout is not inherently incorrect).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] TagDevice now returns the tagDeviceUI error instead of only logging it, so any DB failure in the UI-tagging path propagates out of TagDevice on the synchronous request path. Combined with the now-synchronous call in client.go, a transient anon_device DB error (previously a debug log plus successful auth) now surfaces as a logged warning per request but, for any future caller that checks the error, turns a degraded-tagging condition into an auth-path error; the behavior change from debug-log to returned error is unhandled by the only caller's non-limit branch.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show a behavior change: in `impl.go` `TagDevice` now `return err` when `tagDeviceUI` fails (previously it only logged a debug message and continued). Also `client.go` changed from an async goroutine to a synchronous `TagDevice(ctx, ...)` call. However, the finding’s claim that this is “unhandled by the only caller's non-limit branch” isn’t accurate: `Authenticate` explicitly ignores non-`ErrDeviceLimitReached` errors (it logs a warning and still returns an anonymous identity). So this does not currently turn UI-tagging DB failures into auth failures, though it does change error semantics/logging and could matter for other callers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The device-limit check is a check-then-act race: CountDevices is read outside any transaction with the subsequent insert, so concurrent anonymous requests can all observe count < deviceLimit and insert, exceeding the configured limit. Operators setting device_limit get a soft limit that overshoots under bursty anonymous traffic; there is no unique constraint or atomic guard enforcing the cap, and the overshoot is silent (no log when it happens).

adjudication.rationale: In `AnonDBStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`, the limit enforcement is implemented as a classic check-then-act sequence: it calls `CountDevices(...)` and, only if `count >= s.deviceLimit`, it switches to `s.updateDevice(...)`; otherwise it proceeds to insert/upsert. This count is done outside any transaction or atomic DB constraint guarding the subsequent insert, so concurrent requests can all observe `count < deviceLimit` and then each insert, exceeding the configured cap. The diff shows no unique constraint/locking mechanism to enforce the cap atomically, so the finding’s race/overshoot concern is directly grounded in the new logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] CountDevices is executed on every CreateOrUpdateDevice call whenever deviceLimit > 0, adding an unconditional count query (a full scan over the 30-day window rows on large deployments) to the per-request path. Deployments with millions of anon_device rows pay a counted range scan per anonymous request before any cache/local-cache check short-circuits the write; the count is not cached or rate-limited, so the limit feature converts anonymous auth into count-query amplification proportional to traffic.

adjudication.rationale: In `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go`, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` now does `if s.deviceLimit > 0 { count, err := s.CountDevices(...) ... }` on every call before attempting the upsert. This introduces an extra DB count query on the hot path whenever the feature is enabled, and the diff shows no caching/rate-limiting of that count. The finding’s broader claim about occurring “before any cache/local-cache check short-circuits the write” is not fully verifiable from this diff alone (the local-cache logic isn’t shown here), but the added per-call `CountDevices` overhead itself is clearly diff-grounded and actionable as a performance/architecture concern rather than a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] anonymousDeviceLimit is serialized into frontend settings but nothing in this diff consumes it client-side, so the setting ships inert on the frontend. The value is broadcast to every browser session with no reader; if a UI limit indicator was intended, it is absent, and the field will either rot or require a follow-up to become usable — meanwhile the setting is already fully server-enforced.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `AnonymousDeviceLimit` to `FrontendSettingsDTO` and populates it in `getFrontendSettings` (Go), and adds `anonymousDeviceLimit` to the TS `GrafanaConfig`/`GrafanaBootConfig`. Within this diff there is no client-side logic that reads/uses this value (no UI indicator, no conditional behavior), while the limit is already enforced server-side in `AnonDBStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` via `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit`. That makes the frontend serialization plausibly unnecessary/unused and potentially prone to rotting, but it’s not a correctness defect by itself.
